set.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether using cannabis makes people more likely to go on to other illegal drugs (the 'gateway' idea), or whether the usual order of first use, and the link between the two, come from a shared liability to use drugs and from which drugs people are offered first. In several observational samples, cannabis use usually came before other illegal drugs and was associated with more use of them. The order differed across countries, including some with moderate cannabis use; these patterns alone do not identify a cause. In New York State public high schools in 1971–1973 (5,468 students linked over 5 to 6 months, 66% of the students surveyed in the fall; students who could not be linked had used more drugs), 26% of the 558 students whose drug use had reached cannabis went on to another illegal drug within 5 to 6 months, mostly pills (12 percentage points) or psychedelics (9), with heroin about 2, against 4% of 2,911 students who had used only legal drugs and 1% of 482 who had used none; 56% stayed at cannabis and 19% used only legal drugs in the interval. These percentages were weighted for the survey design and response, not adjusted for other characteristics. The paper calls cannabis a crucial step in both the abstract and the body, but also says a drug does not invariably lead to the next and that the stages are probably culturally determined (Kandel, 1975). In four US household surveys (1991–1994; 44,624 people aged 12 to 25; ages recalled in whole years; people compared within neighbourhood and survey year, with sex, race or ethnicity and age group adjusted for, plus age at first cannabis use in the cocaine models, but without individual-liability covariates in the described analysis), people who had used cannabis were more likely to have had a first chance to try cocaine (relative risk 4.6, 95% CI 3.8 to 5.6, without alcohol or tobacco use; 7.6, 6.9 to 8.4, with it; against people who had used none of the three) and, once offered, about 15 times as likely to start as people who had not used cannabis, regardless of alcohol or tobacco history (11.3 to 19.8), also when the 73% who reported starting at the same age as their first offer were left out (20.4, 10.2 to 40.7); this exclusion also removed people who accepted an unbidden offer at once, so it did not isolate active drug-seeking; about half of the people who had used cannabis started cocaine within 2 years of a first offer, against under 10% of the others many years later (Wagner & Anthony, 2002). In Australian twins born 1964–1971 (311 same-sex pairs in which one twin, but not the other, recalled first using cannabis before 17; interviewed at about 30), the twin who started early more often reported later use of other drugs (for example cocaine or other stimulants 47.9% against 26.4%, conditional odds ratio 4.19, 95% CI 2.60 to 6.75; hallucinogens 5.15; sedatives 2.83; opioids 2.57); the odds ratios stayed between 2.3 and 5.2 after adjustment for measured differences between the twins, and between 2.3 and 3.9 (unadjusted) in the 234 pairs in which both twins had used cannabis. The within-pair comparison accounts for shared rearing, but identical and fraternal pairs were pooled, so genetic confounding is controlled only partly. Separate identical-pair estimates were not printed; peer affiliation and temperament were not described as measured covariates in this paper, without establishing what the broader register measured; the authors call the results consistent with a causal role, perhaps through the social setting of cannabis use and access to other drugs, and say that strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn from them alone (Lynskey et al., 2003). A simulation of US young people, calibrated to household surveys of 1982–1994, in which one shared liability brings forward both the chances to use and the use of all drugs and cannabis has no effect by design, reported a strong relative risk of using heroin, cocaine or hallucinogens (157 in the model, against 24 in the surveys). The survey ratio compares use of those drugs by 21 between people who had and had not used cannabis by 21, without requiring cannabis first; the model’s description also uses prior-initiation wording, so the two ratios may not measure exactly the same quantity. The model also produced an order in which those drugs rarely come first (11 per 1,000, against 16 in the surveys) and a rise with cannabis frequency, and adjusting for an imperfect measure of that liability left large associations; it shows that these patterns cannot by themselves identify a cause, but it was not compared with a model that includes one, and its authors think something like a gateway effect probably exists through contact with illegal markets (Morral et al., 2002). In the 17-country WHO programme (2001–2005; ages recalled at one interview), the order varied across countries alongside how common each drug was. Among people who had used other illegal drugs by 29, cannabis had not already been used at their first other-drug use in 11.4% in the USA and 12.7% in New Zealand, against 83.2% in Japan and 77.8% in Nigeria, where cannabis was rare; these definitions include people who never used cannabis. For Japan, Tables 2 and 4 display n entries 16 for other-drug use and 13 for not-already-cannabis histories; for Nigeria,8 and 7. The estimates are weighted cumulative/projected percentages, and the text does not explicitly define those n entries as unweighted observed counts. The percentages should not be rebuilt as simple fractions of those entries. The corresponding proportion was also high in South Africa (59.2%), where the authors call cannabis use moderate, and Mexico (48.4%). The observed correspondence does not show that prevalence caused the order. In pooled interaction models, the link of cannabis with later other drug use was weaker where cannabis was more common, while that of alcohol or tobacco with later other drug use was stronger where those were more common; the Netherlands–USA country contrast alone does not demonstrate that prevalence relationship; and starting in an unusual order was largely unrelated to later dependence (Degenhardt, Dierker, et al., 2010). A narrative review by proponents of a shared liability argues that the order need not reflect causal steps and calls that liability empirically proven. It also argues that the cannabis-to-other-drug association itself is negligible after accounting for cannabis prevalence, citing a book rather than presenting new data for that assertion. It cites classical twin studies but the article body does not discuss discordant co-twin-control evidence (Vanyukov et al., 2012). No study read separated a causal effect, a shared liability and access to drugs in one design, and all their data were collected between 1971 and 2005. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
set.plain: Does using cannabis lead to other drugs? This is not known. In many places studied, most people who used other illegal drugs had used cannabis first. This was not the order for everyone. Cannabis use was also linked to more use of other drugs: in New York schools in the early 1970 s, about 1 in 4 students who had used cannabis tried another illegal drug within 5 to 6 months, against 4 in 100 of those who had used only alcohol or tobacco. In Australian twins, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often used other drugs later than the other twin, The comparison accounts for growing up in the same home, but not all genetic or other differences between twins. A computer model showed that the same pattern appears if some people are simply more likely to use any drug and are offered cannabis first, with no effect of cannabis at all. Across surveys in 17 countries, the order varied. Some people had not used cannabis when they first used another illegal drug, including some who never used cannabis. This was common in some places with rare or moderate cannabis use; the displayed table counts for Japan and Nigeria were small, with their counting basis unclear. No study separated cause, shared risk and access to drugs. See the contested question.
set.magnitude: Not estimable as a causal effect. Kandel (1975), 5–6 months, unadjusted: moved beyond cannabis 26% of 558 students at the cannabis step (pills 12, psychedelics 9, cocaine 2, heroin 2 percentage points) vs 4% of 2,911 who had used only legal drugs and 1% of 482 who had used none; cannabis use during follow-up 27% in the baseline exclusive-legal-drug group currently using beer/wine,cigarettes and hard liquor in the past 30 days (N≥342), versus 2% who had never used any drug at baseline (N≥467). Wagner & Anthony (2002), relative risks (95% CI): first chance to try cocaine, against people who had used none of alcohol, tobacco or cannabis, 1.9 (1.7–2.1) after alcohol or tobacco only, 4.6 (3.8–5.6) after cannabis only, 7.6 (6.9–8.4) after both; starting cocaine once offered, cannabis vs no cannabis, 15 (11.3–19.8), and 20.4 (10.2–40.7) without people who started in the same year as the offer (73% of people who used cocaine); about 50% of people who had used cannabis started within 2 years of a first offer vs under 10% of others many years later. Lynskey et al. (2003), 311 discordant pairs, twin who started cannabis before 17 vs co-twin, lifetime prevalence and conditional odds ratio, unadjusted (adjusted): sedatives 19.0% vs 8.4%, 2.83 (2.28); hallucinogens 35.4% vs 18.0%, 5.15 (5.15); cocaine or other stimulants 47.9% vs 26.4%, 4.19 (4.06); opioids 13.5% vs 6.4%, 2.57 (2.34); in 234 pairs in which both used cannabis, unadjusted 3.00, 3.92, 3.00 and 2.33. Morral et al. (2002), simulation with no gateway effect vs US surveys: reported relative risks 157 vs 24; the survey uses cannabis and other-drug use by 21 without requiring an order, while the model also uses prior-initiation wording, so exact comparability is uncertain; one of those drugs at least a year before cannabis, 11 vs 16 per 1,000; odds ratio 297 with no adjustment, 82 after adjustment for a liability indicator correlated 0.8 with the liability (64% variance in a simple linear reading; editors’0.8² calculation, not 80%); no uncertainty intervals. Degenhardt, Dierker, et al. (2010): people who had not already used cannabis when starting other illegal drugs by 29 (including never-cannabis use), USA 11.4%, New Zealand 12.7%, Japan 83.2% and Nigeria 77.8%; the displayed Table 2/Table 4 n entries are 16/13 and 8/7, respectively, and their basis is not explicitly labelled unweighted observed counts; the weighted cumulative/projected percentages are not simple fractions of these entries; cannabis and later other illegal drugs at 18–29, odds ratio 7.4 (1.8–30.4) in the Netherlands vs 107.1 (57.9–198.1) in the USA; pooled interaction of cannabis use with cannabis prevalence 0.3 (0.2–0.6), of alcohol or tobacco use with their prevalence 32.7 (8.3–129.0), scale not stated.

risk_of_bias.note: No individual-liability covariates were included in the described analyses in the school panel or the surveys (cards sc_kandel_1975: ROBINS-E, very high, no confounder adjustment despite survey weighting and a third of the panel lost, more of them people who used drugs; sc_wagner_2002 and sc_degenhardt_2010 a: high); the co-twin study cannot exclude factors that differ between co-twins and shows no identical-pair estimates (sc_lynskey_2003: high); the simulation's assumptions are untested and it was not compared with a model that includes a gateway effect (sc_morral_2002: high); the review is an argued position without search or appraisal (sc_vanyukov_2012: high).

inconsistency.note: The strength of the link varies widely between countries (cannabis and later other illegal drugs at 18–29, odds ratio 7.4 in the Netherlands against 107.1 in the USA), non-cannabis-first histories also occur where cannabis use is moderate; they include never-cannabis use, and the designs address different parts of the causal question: a co-twin comparison finds a link beyond shared family factors, while a model with no effect of cannabis reproduces the population patterns.

indirectness.note: All data were collected between 1971 and 2005, mostly in the USA and Australia; the cross-national surveys show that the pattern varies across places and cohorts, so it may differ in other places and in later years, including where cannabis is sold legally (not studied in the papers read).

imprecision.note: Large surveys and twin intervals that exclude 1; the Japan and Nigeria proportions have small displayed table counts (16 and 8 for other-drug use), whose count basis is not fully explained, and are used only to illustrate different histories; the simulation gives no intervals.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence and a simulation start low; down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness: very low, the floor. The claim concerns cause, so its relation is insufficient evidence; that cannabis use usually comes first and goes with a higher chance of using other illegal drugs is reported in it, not rated as a separate claim. Counted once: Wagner & Anthony (1991–1994) and Morral et al. (1982–1994) draw on the same series of US household surveys; Vanyukov et al. add no data and cite Morral et al. and Degenhardt, Dierker, et al.; the WHO surveys include the US and New Zealand surveys whose earlier analyses the paper cites. Status contested: a co-twin comparison and survey analyses point to a link beyond shared family factors and beyond being offered, while a model and cross-national data show that a shared liability and access can produce the same patterns, so the six-part debate box applies.

debate.question: Does using cannabis make people more likely to go on to other illegal drugs, or do the usual order and the link come from a shared liability to use drugs and from which drugs people are offered first?
debate.evidence_yes: In Australian twins born 1964–1971, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often went on to use other drugs than the co-twin who did not (conditional odds ratios 2.57 to 5.15; for example cocaine or other stimulants 47.9% against 26.4%), also after adjustment for measured differences between the twins (2.3 to 5.2) and in pairs in which both twins had used cannabis (2.3 to 3.9); the comparison accounts for shared rearing, with only partial genetic control when identical and fraternal pairs are pooled (Lynskey et al., 2003). In US household surveys of 1991–1994, people who had used cannabis were more likely to be offered cocaine (relative risks 4.6 to 7.6) and, once offered, about 15 times as likely to start, also when people who reported starting at the same age as the offer were left out (20.4), with people compared within the same neighbourhood and survey year (Wagner & Anthony, 2002). Cannabis came before other illegal drugs for most people in most places studied; in 1971–1973 about a quarter of New York State students at the cannabis step went on to another illegal drug within 5 to 6 months, against 4% of students who had used only legal drugs (Kandel, 1975); and in nearly every one of 17 countries, starting a drug earlier in the usual sequence went with much higher odds of starting a later one (Degenhardt, Dierker, et al., 2010). Routes proposed but not tested include the social setting in which cannabis is used, lower perceived risk, and access to other drugs through people who sell cannabis (Lynskey et al., 2003; Morral et al., 2002).
debate.evidence_no: A simulation in which one shared liability, and the order in which drugs are offered, drive all first use, with no effect of cannabis by design, reproduced the patterns usually cited for a gateway: large printed relative risks (157 in the model and 24 in US surveys), whose exact comparability is unsettled because the survey counts use by 21 without requiring cannabis first while the model also uses prior-initiation wording, an order in which heroin, cocaine or hallucinogens rarely come first (11 against 16 per 1,000) and a rise with cannabis frequency; adjusting for an imperfect measure of that liability left large associations (an odds ratio of 297 fell only to 82 with an indicator correlated 0.8 with liability, corresponding to 64% variance in a simple linear reading (editors’ squared-correlation calculation)), so adjustment of the kind used in observational studies cannot rule a shared liability out (Morral et al., 2002). Across the WHO surveys the order varied alongside differences in prevalence: histories without cannabis already used were common in Japan and Nigeria, where cannabis was rare and the estimates rested on few people, and in South Africa, where use was moderate. These histories include never-cannabis use; the link of cannabis with later other drug use was weaker where cannabis was common; and starting out of order did not go with more dependence (Degenhardt, Dierker, et al., 2010). In 1971–1973, most New York State students at the cannabis step did not move on within 5 to 6 months (56% stayed at cannabis, 19% used only legal drugs in the interval), the author wrote that the stages are probably culturally determined, and the percentages were survey-weighted without covariate adjustment (Kandel, 1975). The US survey analysis places part of the link at being offered cocaine, which fits access as well as an effect of cannabis, and measured no individual liability (Wagner & Anthony, 2002). Proponents of a shared liability argue that the order follows how available and common each drug is and that the stages are defined circularly (Vanyukov et al., 2012).
debate.neither_can_show: None of these studies randomly assigned cannabis use. The school panel and the household surveys rest on self-reports, mostly ages recalled years later in whole years, and did not include individual-liability covariates in the described analyses; the co-twin design accounts for shared rearing but, with fraternal and identical twins pooled, not all genetic or other differences between them (friends, temperament, their own early behaviour), and the study read shows no separate results for identical twins; a simulation shows what a model can produce, not what happened. The cross-national comparison rests on differences between countries that also differ in law, drug markets and willingness to report use. None of the designs separates an effect of cannabis itself from the effect of buying it where other drugs are sold, and all the data were collected between 1971 and 2005.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). Several observational samples show cannabis usually coming first and an association with other-drug use; histories without cannabis already used are also common in some countries with moderate use. The narrative review disputes the association itself, without presenting new data to establish its asserted negligible size; that a shared liability and the order in which drugs are offered can produce this pattern without any effect of cannabis is shown by a model; and that the link persists within twin pairs shows that the family background twins share does not explain all of it. The evidence read cannot say whether the remaining link is an effect of cannabis, of access to illegal markets, or of differences between twins, and in the one study that followed students over a few months, about 3 in 4 students at the cannabis step did not move on to another illegal drug within 5 to 6 months.
debate.what_would_settle_it: A cohort followed from before any drug use, recording offers and first use of each drug as they happen, with liability measured beforehand (behaviour, family and friends' use) and the local availability of each drug, and with enough identical twin pairs who differ in cannabis use to give separate estimates; and natural experiments that change access to cannabis without changing access to other drugs, such as legal sales kept apart from illegal markets, with later use of other drugs measured.

set.statement: As summarized in two narrative reviews, whose figures are second-hand and come from studies for which the reviews report no formal appraisal, using more than one drug is common among people who use illegal drugs, how common depends on who was asked and how use was defined, and it makes the long-term effects of any one drug hard to study in people. Studies define it as using several drugs over a period (lifetime, or the past 1 to 12 months) or on the same occasion, the second being hard to capture in surveys and mostly studied in smaller high-risk samples, although the review also describes national survey work that measured same-occasion use; the historical DSM diagnosis of polysubstance dependence was dropped from DSM-5, and most population research records only how often each drug is used. Studies that group people by the drugs they use typically find a limited range (alcohol, tobacco, cannabis), a moderate range (adding amphetamine-type drugs) and an extended range (adding prescription drugs used non-medically and other illegal drugs). Limited-range use was reported by 18% of 12- to 17-year-olds (ever) and by 34% of teenagers before 16, in two samples; extended-range use by 2% of 12- to 17-year-olds and 13.5% of 18- to 29-year-olds in Australian national samples, two different age groups that the review calls panel designs; and up to 75% of people at underground raves used several drugs, on average five at the last rave. Classes with a wide range of use reported more psychological distress, anxiety and depression in the cited studies; several imaging studies and studies of inhibitory control and decision-making found no difference in performance from comparison groups, while another study reported large differences on standard tests outside the scanner and a metabolite study linked brain measures with memory performance. The findings were mixed, although the review’s conclusion states cognitive deficits as clear; and the authors judged research on preventing and treating the use of several drugs underdeveloped (Connor et al., 2014). In the ecstasy research reviewed in 2006, the great majority of people who used it also used other drugs, most often alcohol, cannabis and stimulants: earlier studies found cannabis use in 90% to 100% of people who used ecstasy, and in one survey everyone new to ecstasy (1 to 9 pills in all) had smoked cannabis in the previous month, 32% on five or more occasions. Studies that compared people who use ecstasy with people who use no drugs therefore make it difficult to separate ecstasy from other drug effects; in studies with comparison groups who used other drugs but not ecstasy (samples described as up to 234, without resolving whether this counts only people using ecstasy or all comparison groups), raised psychological problems went with drug use in general rather than with ecstasy, though those comparison groups mostly used drugs more moderately; some earlier studies did not record other drugs; and findings on whether cannabis explains, adds to or offsets problems seen in people who use ecstasy pointed in different directions. The reviewers propose following large cohorts of young people who are not or not yet using drugs and may belong to risk groups, for years, with drug histories recorded and psychological and cognitive tests repeated (Gouzoulis-Mayfrank & Daumann, 2006). How often people who use cocaine also drink or use cannabis, and what that means for cocaine research, is in the answer on cocaine with alcohol and cannabis. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.

risk_of_bias.note: Both sources are narrative reviews without reported systematic search methods or formal appraisal (cards sc_connor_2014 and sc_gouzoulis_mayfrank_2006: editors' checklist, high), each drawing partly on its authors' own studies; the primary studies cannot be appraised here (METHODS §6.3).

inconsistency.note: The figures differ widely by population (2% of 12- to 17-year-olds with extended-range use, up to 75% of people at underground raves using several drugs), as the claim states; in every sample of people who use illegal drugs that the reviews describe (people at raves, people who use ecstasy), using several drugs is common.

indirectness.note: All figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3), mostly from Australian and US samples around 2013 and from the ecstasy research reviewed in 2006.

imprecision.note: No intervals are given; the figures are presented as descriptions of the samples, not as population estimates.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim resting only on two narrative reviews: it starts low (the descriptive quantities used here come from observational survey samples), is rated down one level for risk of bias (not appraisable) and one for indirectness (second-hand): very low; it stays at draft and out of the at-a-glance box (METHODS §6.3). The two reviews come from different groups, in Queensland in 2014 and in Cologne in 2006, and describe different primary studies; those of people who use illegal drugs all show that using several drugs is common: status replicated, as a description of those samples, not of any population. The first review reports health and cognitive associations, with mixed cognitive findings and no design inventory; these are described, not rated as causal effects; its 2% and 13.5% compare different age groups in different samples, not the same people over time (card reporting issue). The cocaine figures (Liu et al., 2018) belong to the cocaine answer and are neither repeated nor counted here.
